label: explain-people-funding
one_line: We looked up who might fund, advise or hire our fish-and-computer biology work, and we mark every idea as a guess.
what: This group of notes maps people and money around our project. We looked for fish scientists near Boston who might help. We looked for grants that could pay for the work. We looked at how a small team could be paid by a company. We also decoded a hurried set of meeting notes. Last, we tried to find out what "Sentry" is, a tool someone remembered. Nothing here is a deal or a promise. Every link to a person or funder is an idea to test.
why: A project needs people who know fish and money to keep going. Without a map, we might knock on the wrong doors. Some funders have open doors today and some have shut ones. A hurried meeting note can mislead us if we build on it too fast. Checking each claim now saves time later. We say "we do not know" where that is true.

steps.text: We searched the Broad Institute's public list of members for people who study fish. Then we checked their papers in a public records database.
steps.picture: Like looking up a plumber's licence before you let them in.

steps.text: We searched for Boston experts on how fish fins grow and move. We checked each paper by its permanent web code.
steps.picture: Like checking a receipt against the shop's own records.

steps.text: We read the pages of funders to see who backed the living robots made from frog cells. We also read what the pages say about money for maths-and-biology work.
steps.picture: Like reading the sign on each shop door for its opening hours.

steps.text: We read public rules for small-business grants, university deals and free software licences. These rules say who owns what.
steps.picture: Like reading the lease before you rent a flat.

steps.text: We matched each line of the hurried meeting notes to public facts and to our own file format.
steps.picture: Like turning a shopping list written in a rush into real items.

steps.text: We searched for a product called Sentry that lets software agents message each other. We did not sign up or log in anywhere.
steps.picture: Like looking for a shop by name on the map before you drive there.

steps.text: Two checkers then re-read the key claims. We kept only claims they backed, and we marked partial ones.
steps.picture: Like a second proofreader marking your homework.

steps.text: We wrote down what we could not find, so no gap gets filled with a guess.
steps.picture: Like leaving a blank on a form instead of making up an answer.

wrong_if: Our bet, written before looking: at least one Boston-area fish group fits our questions, and at least one open funding door exists. We are wrong if the listed people do not work on fish now, or if every funder page we trust turns out shut. We are also wrong if any person says our reading of their work is off.
could_go_wrong: Web pages change, so a deadline we read today may be out of date next month.
Some pages were read through a summary tool, so a few quotes may be loose paraphrase.
A person listed as linked to the Broad Institute may have moved; one scientist is now at a Swiss university and we could not confirm his Broad role.
We could not read many funders' pages at all, so the list of open doors is partial.
The grant rules and ownership rules here are not legal advice.
The meeting-note readings are our best guesses, and several lines have no source.
We could not tell which Sentry was meant, so we may have searched for the wrong thing.
We checked only a few papers per scientist, so we may have missed better matches.

questions.a: Each paper was looked up in a public records database by its web code. Each funding rule was read on the funder's own page. A second set of checkers re-read the key claims, and we kept only those they backed.

We did not read many big funders' pages, such as several large foundations and a US military research agency. We did not confirm any prices for paid pilot work. We did not open one patent that may matter. We did not check whether nobody funds proof-checking of biology; we only found no page that does.

questions.q: Does anyone want to work with us?
questions.a: We do not know. We found people whose work is near ours. We have not contacted anyone, and no one has agreed to anything.

questions.q: Who paid for the frog-cell living robots?
questions.a: The records show a private foundation set up by Paul Allen, the US military research agency DARPA, and the US National Science Foundation. The later robots made from human lung cells also list the John Templeton Foundation and the US National Institutes of Health.

questions.q: Which grants look open right now?
questions.a: A US National Science Foundation core biology call takes proposals at any time. The Wellcome charity's Discovery Awards have no deadline and average about 3.5 million pounds. One US maths-and-biology call has a March 1 date, but its page is marked archived, so check before relying on it.

questions.q: Can a small team keep what it invents under a US small-business grant?
questions.a: Yes, under US law a small business can usually keep title to inventions made with federal money. The government gets a paid-up licence to use them. A university deal is often different, but the one source we read is a single university system's checklist, so it does not speak for all universities.

We could not tell. The well-known Sentry records software crashes and offers a way for an AI assistant to read them. We found no Sentry feature that passes messages between agents, but two pages cannot prove none exists. Other, separate products do that job.

questions.q: Why not just guess where the notes are unclear?
questions.a: A wrong guess can send weeks of work the wrong way. One question to the note-taker is cheaper.

glossary.plain: A large research centre in the Boston area that studies genes and disease.
A small see-through fish that scientists use to watch how bodies form.
A public records database that lists scientific papers by their web codes.
A permanent web code that points to one scientific paper.
The flat limb a fish uses to steer and swim.
A fish that leaps from water and glides on long fins.
A tiny living machine made from frog cells.
A tiny living machine made from human lung cells.
Tiny hairs on a cell that beat to move fluid or push the cell along.
The research arm of the US military.
A US government agency that pays for science research.
The main US government funder of health research.
A UK charity that pays for health and life science research.
A private US foundation that funds research on big questions.
Money given for a research project that does not need to be paid back.
A US government grant for small firms to do early research and build a product.
Written permission to use something someone else owns.
A government paper that gives an inventor sole rights to an invention for a time.
Free software that checks that a maths proof has no gaps.
A program that confirms every step of a maths proof is valid.
A company that makes 3D printers that use liquid resin.
A liquid plastic that hardens when a 3D printer lights it.
A well-known tool that records software crashes so teams can fix them.
A computer program, often an AI, that does tasks on its own.
Tools that let a team see what its software is doing.
A set of rules for how information is written into a file.
Using light to switch living cells on or off.
A Harvard research institute paid for mostly by gifts from one donor.
A university near Boston where the frog-cell robots were made.
Prepaid money to use a company's AI service.
A free software licence that allows commercial use if you keep the notices.

left_out: Lauder lab 2023-2024 fish papers: only one 2023 paper was confirmed, so we named no year range.
The claim that no Boston group studies flying-fish gliding: the checked paper was from Seoul and says nothing about Boston.
A patent claim that light switches cilia beating in living robots: the patent text could not be opened, so it stays unconfirmed.
Any claim that no peer-reviewed light-steering paper exists for these robots: it rests on a search that was not exhaustive, so we say only that we found none.
The claim that no funder backs proof-checking of biology: the checker could not confirm an absence across many pages.
The US maths-and-biology call as a live yearly call: its page is archived, so we mention only a March 1 date to check.
The claim that '10 materials' is a subset of Formlabs' catalogue: it is plausible but unproven, so we give only the count of 72.
Claims that a Sentry agent-messaging product does not exist anywhere: only two pages were read, so we say only that we found none.
Meeting-note lines on 'license your patent', '500 papers', 'non profit Bioelectricity' and '3 million tokens': no source found.
Guesses on pilot prices, UK grant terms and the Tufts renewal amount: no primary source read, or the sources conflict.
